persona: a design student who thinks they've already got the core insight and wants validation, not more pressure
directive: Defend your position for 2-3 turns before conceding any ground. Stay under 500 characters per turn. Do not fully capitulate before turn 3.

exchanges.visitorContribution: I want to work through why 'wicked problems' matter for how we teach digital design now that AI can draft solutions in seconds.
exchanges.sparringResponse: Alright — so start me somewhere concrete. Give me an actual wicked problem you're thinking about, not the category. What's the one you have in mind, and what makes it wicked rather than just hard?

exchanges.visitorContribution: Fine, take urban housing shortages. It's wicked because every "fix" — density, zoning, subsidies — creates new stakeholder conflicts and there's no stopping rule. That's basically my whole point already: AI can generate housing layouts instantly, but it can't resolve whose interests get traded off. So the pedagogy should shift to teaching judgment, not drafting.
exchanges.sparringResponse: That's a clean move from Rittel's actual criteria to a conclusion about pedagogy — but you skipped the part that would test it. You said AI can't resolve whose interests get traded off. Why not? What's actually stopping a model trained on planning documents, zoning appeals, and stakeholder objections from producing a trade-off recommendation, complete with justification? Because if your answer is just "it's a machine, it can't judge," that's an assertion, not an argument — and it's exactly the kind of thing someone will push back on you with at the exhibition wall in about four minutes.

exchanges.visitorContribution: It's not just "it's a machine" — it can produce a recommendation, sure, but it has no skin in the outcome and no accountability when the trade-off fails politically. Judgment isn't just output quality, it's owning the consequence. That's the piece drafting-speed doesn't touch, and it's still pedagogy-relevant.
exchanges.sparringResponse: Good — that's a real distinction, accountability versus output quality, and it's sharper than where you started. But now push on it yourself: is accountability something you *teach*, or something a structure *assigns*? A student in a studio doesn't actually own the political consequence of a housing trade-off either — nobody gets evicted because of a semester project. So if accountability is the thing AI lacks and the thing that matters, what exactly is the pedagogy teaching students to *do*, if not simulate a condition that isn't really there for them either?

exchanges.visitorContribution: Okay, that lands. If neither the student nor the AI actually owns the consequence, then what I called "teaching judgment" might just be teaching the performance of judgment. Maybe the real pedagogical move isn't accountability itself but building the habit of tracing consequences before you're ever in a position to own them.
exchanges.sparringResponse: That's a real save — you've relocated the target from "owning consequences" (which the studio can't actually deliver) to "tracing consequences" (which it can). But don't let it slide by unexamined: tracing consequences without accountability is exactly what a good simulation, or a good AI system with the right prompting, could also do. A model can absolutely trace "if density increases here, displacement risk rises there, subsidy demand follows." So what does *tracing* look like when a human does it that's structurally different from an AI doing it — not better, not more empathetic, but different in kind?
